bottleneck: HIV integrates as provirus into long-lived memory T cells and other reservoirs where antiretrovirals cannot reach. CRISPR excision must find every proviral copy — missing even a few lets the virus rebound — while avoiding off-target cuts across the T-cell genome. Latently infected cells are rare, scattered, and indistinguishable from healthy ones, so delivery cannot target them specifically, and the virus's own mutation rate generates escape variants around any single guide.
current_state: Excision works in cell models and reduces provirus in animals, but complete reservoir clearance in vivo has never been demonstrated. Combination guides and improved delivery are in preclinical testing.

sources.title: CRISPR Unleashed: Engineering Our Next-Gen Antivirals

title: HIV provirus excision cannot clear every reservoir cell
why_it_blocks: HIV cure requires 100% — a single surviving provirus restarts infection. The completeness requirement makes excision the hardest possible editing task, demanding perfection across billions of cells.
